question: State two actions to preserve a seized mobile device for forensic analysis.

points: Retain the current power state/status if possible (1)
Isolate the device from the network/communications (1)
Keep chargers and cables with the device (1)
Use a Faraday bag/cage or disable wireless communication (1)
Document the chain of custody (1)

question: Explain how an investigator should isolate a device that is suspected of communicating so that evidence is preserved.

points: Photograph the screen first to capture what is displayed (1)
Turn off the device or remove the battery/power cable (1)
Use airplane mode or disable wireless communication (1)
Place the device in a Faraday bag/cage to block signals (1)

question: Explain the importance of documenting the chain of custody when collecting forensic evidence.

points: The chain of custody records everyone who handled the evidence, when and what they did (1)
It proves the evidence has not been altered or tampered with (1)
An unbroken chain is required for evidence to be admissible in court (1)
Any gap or inconsistency can make the evidence inadmissible (1)

topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — live forensics
question: Explain two challenges of performing live forensics on a running system.

points: Data is changing in situ — files and memory are being modified while examined (1)
Recovering corrupted data and preventing further corruption is difficult (1)
Capturing data in active memory must be done quickly before it is lost (1)
Remote data must be captured over the network, and temporary files must not be lost (1)

topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — network forensics
question: Explain the steps required before scanning a network for forensic analysis.

points: Agree a network-testing forensics methodology with supervisory and investigatory authorities (1)
Ensure permission is granted to carry out the scan (1)
Ensure the testing protocol will not disrupt a live system (1)
Use passive and active analysis tools appropriately (1)

topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — network forensics
question: Describe the network infrastructure that an investigator would review during network forensics.

points: Firewalls and infrastructure devices — switches, routers, wireless access points (1)
Client or server logs (1)
Malware activity and alerts (1)

topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — documenting the scene
question: Describe how an investigator documents the scene of an incident.

points: Prior planning for a range of scenarios (1)
Securing the scene (1)
Plans, photos and diagrams of the scene (1)
Contemporaneous notes (1)
Witness statements (1)

question: Explain why a hash/checksum is generated for a forensic copy of a system.

points: A hash (checksum) is a digital fingerprint of the data (1)
It proves the forensic copy is an exact match of the original (1)
If the hash changes, it shows the data has been altered (1)
This maintains evidence integrity and admissibility (1)

question: State two requirements for recording forensic findings reliably.

points: No action should change the data on the digital device (1)
Collection must be done by a competent person (1)
A trail/record of all actions taken must be created (1)
Documentation of who is responsible for collection/decisions (1)

question: Explain why an investigator should work with copies/images rather than original data.

points: Working on the original could alter the evidence (1)
Altered data may be inadmissible in court (1)
Using copies preserves the original unchanged (1)
All alterations (intentional or unintentional) must be documented (1)

question: State two forms of visual evidence created during forensic analysis.

points: Photos (1)
Videos (1)
Screenshots (1)
Date-time stamps and metadata (1)

question: Explain how an investigator ensures findings are relevant and not false positives.

points: Define file signatures and search criteria carefully (1)
Know the error rates of the tools and data types used (1)
Feed back false-positive data to improve the detection method (1)
Manually review all positives and further investigate filtered positives (1)

question: State two things an investigator assesses findings for.

points: Evidence of a crime and/or an incident (1)
A regulatory breach (1)
Civil liability or contractual breach (1)
Non-compliance with internal policy (1)
Negligence or mismanagement (1)

question: Describe three indicators that a system has been compromised.

points: Unusual traffic — inbound, outbound or from unusual geographical regions (1)
Unusual login attempts or DNS requests (1)
Increase in file/data reads or requests (1)
Unusual port usage (1)
Suspicious changes to or access to files/data (1)

question: Explain the structure and purpose of a security report written after an incident.

points: A clear structure — title, contents, introduction, headings, numbered/bulleted points, conclusions, footnotes, citations (1)
It analyses the incident to identify errors/omissions in procedures (1)
It identifies errors/delays in detection and remedial actions (1)
It recommends improvements to IT policies and protection measures (physical, software, hardware, processes, training) (1)

question: State two areas of improvement a security report should recommend.

points: Improvements to the content of IT policies (1)
Improvements to physical security measures (1)
Improvements to software or hardware protection (1)
Improvements to processes, procedures and training (1)
